subject: English
description: Comma, semicolon, colon, apostrophe, quotation marks — usage rules

questions.stem: Choose the correctly punctuated sentence:

options.option_text: He bought apples oranges and pears.
He bought apples, oranges, and pears.
He bought, apples oranges, and pears.
He, bought apples oranges and pears.

questions.explanation: Series rule — separate items in a list with commas. The 'Oxford / serial' comma before 'and' (in 'apples, oranges, and pears') is preferred in American English; British English often omits it but never inconsistently. Avoid commas after the verb ('bought,') unless setting off an interrupting phrase. Listing example: 'I want eggs, bread, and milk.' The Oxford comma can also disambiguate — 'I love my parents, Lady Gaga, and Humpty Dumpty' vs 'I love my parents, Lady Gaga and Humpty Dumpty' (the latter implies they ARE her parents).
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the apostrophe correctly?

options.option_text: The dog wagged it's tail.
The dog wagged its tail.
The dogs's tail wagged.
The dog wagged its' tail.

questions.explanation: ITS — possessive (no apostrophe; like 'his', 'her'). IT'S — contraction of 'it is' or 'it has'. So 'the dog wagged ITS tail' (possessive). Apostrophe rules: (1) singular noun + 's ('John's car'); (2) plural noun ending in 's' + ' ('dogs' tails'); (3) plural not ending in 's' + 's ('children's books'). Never use apostrophe to make plurals (NOT 'apple's' for two apples — write 'apples').

questions.stem: Identify the SENTENCE that correctly uses a SEMICOLON:

options.option_text: She loves; tea, coffee and milk.
He travelled extensively; he visited Paris, Rome, and Tokyo.
The book is; new.
I went to the; market yesterday.

questions.explanation: Semicolon (;) connects two independent (complete) clauses that are closely related — 'He travelled extensively; he visited Paris...' Both halves can stand alone as sentences. Stronger than a comma but weaker than a full stop. Also used to separate items in a list when the items themselves contain commas — 'We invited Anil, my brother; Beena, my colleague; and Chetan, my friend.' Don't use semicolons after subject ('She loves;') or before adjective ('the book is;').
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correctly placed colon:

options.option_text: She: bought apples and pears.
Three nations attended: India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh.
She bought: apples.
He: like dogs.

questions.explanation: COLON (:) introduces a list, an explanation, an example, or a quotation. The text BEFORE the colon should stand as a complete clause. Correct: 'Three nations attended: India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh.' (the first part is a complete clause). Don't break the verb-object link with a colon — 'She bought: apples' is wrong. Other valid uses: time (10:30), ratio (3:5), Bible references (John 3:16), titles ('The book: a sequel').
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Which sentence handles QUOTATION MARKS correctly (American convention)?

options.option_text: She said "I am tired".
She said, "I am tired."
She said: I am tired.
She said "I am tired";.

questions.explanation: American convention — comma before opening quote; period (or comma) inside the closing quote (always). 'She said, "I am tired."' British convention puts logical punctuation: only marks belonging to the original quoted sentence go inside; otherwise outside. Most exam papers in India follow British convention but accept either. ALWAYS capitalise the first word of a complete quoted sentence: ' "I am tired," she said.'

questions.stem: Pick the sentence with the correct usage of the EM-DASH:

options.option_text: He left—at six o'clock—the office.
Three friends—Aman, Bina, Chetan—came to visit.
She—bought—apples.
He sang—well—the song.

questions.explanation: Em-dash (—) — sets off a parenthetical phrase MORE EMPHATICALLY than commas or parentheses. 'Three friends—Aman, Bina, Chetan—came to visit.' Replaces commas / brackets when you want the interrupting phrase to stand out. Don't break inseparable elements (subject-verb or verb-object) with em-dashes. Hyphen (-) for compound words (well-known); en-dash (–) for ranges (1990–2020). On the keyboard, the em-dash is two hyphens or Alt+0151 / Option-Shift-Hyphen on Mac.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Identify the correctly punctuated sentence with hyphenation:

options.option_text: He is a well known scientist.
He is a well-known scientist (compound modifier before noun).
He is well-known.
He-is-a-well-known scientist.

questions.explanation: Hyphen joins compound modifiers BEFORE a noun: 'a well-known scientist'. AFTER a verb (predicative position), no hyphen is needed: 'The scientist is well known'. Other examples: 'a state-of-the-art lab' but 'the lab is state of the art'. Compound nouns generally take hyphens (mother-in-law, brother-in-law). Numbers — hyphenated when written: 'twenty-one'. Prefixes — usually no hyphen ('pre-school' vs 'preschool' is style-dependent).
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses a comma after an introductory adverbial clause?

options.option_text: Although it rained heavily the match was not cancelled.
Although it rained heavily, the match was not cancelled.
Although, it rained heavily the match was not cancelled.
Although it rained heavily the match, was not cancelled.

questions.explanation: B is correct because a comma must follow an introductory adverbial clause before the main clause begins. Option A omits the required comma — the most common student error. Option C wrongly places the comma after 'Although', splitting the subordinating conjunction from its own clause. Option D inserts the comma between 'match' and its verb, disrupting the main clause's subject–verb unit.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses commas to set off an appositive phrase?

options.option_text: My brother, an IAS officer lives in New Delhi.
My brother an IAS officer, lives in New Delhi.
My brother, an IAS officer, lives in New Delhi.
My brother an IAS officer lives in New Delhi.

questions.explanation: A non-restrictive appositive phrase ('an IAS officer') must be enclosed by commas on both sides to signal it is supplementary information. C does this correctly. Option A omits the closing comma; Option B omits the opening comma; Option D omits both — each failure blurs where the appositive begins or ends and is marked wrong in SSC/IBPS answer keys.

questions.stem: In which sentence does the omission of the Oxford (serial) comma create genuine ambiguity about the number of people being thanked?

options.option_text: I bought apples, oranges and bananas from the vendor.
She thanked her parents, the Principal and the Chief Guest.
We need pens, pencils and erasers for tomorrow's test.
The panel includes Ravi, Suresh and Mahesh as nominees.

questions.explanation: B is ambiguous without the Oxford comma: 'her parents, the Principal and the Chief Guest' allows an appositive reading in which 'the Principal and the Chief Guest' identifies who her parents are — reducing three people to one. Adding the comma ('parents, the Principal, and the Chief Guest') unambiguously lists three separate people. In A, C, and D the list items are clearly distinct entities with no apposition risk.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses parentheses to expand an abbreviation inline?

options.option_text: The RBI (Reserve Bank of India), was established in 1935.
The RBI (Reserve Bank of India) was established in 1935.
The RBI, (Reserve Bank of India) was established in 1935.
The (RBI) Reserve Bank of India was established in 1935.

questions.explanation: B is correct: the expansion immediately follows the abbreviation inside parentheses with no intervening punctuation, and sentence punctuation resumes normally after the closing parenthesis. Option A wrongly adds a comma after the closing parenthesis as though it were a non-restrictive clause. Option C inserts a comma before the opening parenthesis — never standard. Option D reverses the order; the abbreviation must precede its expansion.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a comma splice (i.e., correctly punctuates two independent clauses)?

options.option_text: She studied all night, she passed the examination easily.
He was exhausted, however he kept working through the night.
The results were announced; many students celebrated outside.
It was raining heavily, they cancelled the cricket fixture.

questions.explanation: C correctly uses a semicolon to join two related but grammatically independent clauses — the standard remedy for a comma splice. Options A and D are straightforward comma splices. Option B is the subtler trap: 'however' is a conjunctive adverb, not a coordinating conjunction, so it requires a semicolon before it ('exhausted; however, he kept working'), not merely a comma — making B a comma splice as well.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly punctuates the conjunctive adverb 'therefore' when it links two independent clauses?

options.option_text: He prepared thoroughly, therefore he cleared the prelims.
He prepared thoroughly; therefore, he cleared the prelims.
He prepared thoroughly therefore; he cleared the prelims.
He prepared thoroughly therefore, he cleared the prelims.

questions.explanation: The rule for conjunctive adverbs (therefore, however, consequently) is: semicolon before + comma after. B applies this exactly: 'thoroughly; therefore, he cleared'. Option A uses only a comma before 'therefore' — a classic comma splice. Option C places the semicolon after 'therefore', incorrectly severing it from the clause it introduces. Option D has no semicolon at all, producing yet another comma splice with a misplaced comma.

questions.stem: Identify the sentence in which the period is placed INCORRECTLY relative to the closing parenthesis.

options.option_text: She topped the exam (her highest score to date).
She topped the exam. (It was her highest score to date.)
She topped the exam (her highest score to date.)
He left at noon; she stayed on (as per the roster).

questions.explanation: When a parenthetical phrase is embedded within a larger sentence (not a standalone sentence), the period belongs outside the closing parenthesis. C wrongly places the period inside — 'to date.' — even though the parenthetical is a phrase, not an independent sentence. Option A correctly places the period outside. Option B is also correct: here the parenthetical is a full standalone sentence following a complete sentence, so its own period sits inside the parentheses. Option D likewise correctly keeps the period outside a mid-sentence phrase.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly places a comma after an introductory adverbial clause?

options.option_text: When the results were announced the students cheered.
When the results were announced, the students cheered.
When, the results were announced the students cheered.
When the results were announced the students, cheered.

questions.explanation: B is correct because a dependent adverbial clause that opens a sentence must be separated from the main clause by a comma. A omits this comma entirely, fusing dependent and main clauses without a break. C wrongly inserts the comma inside the subordinating clause after 'When'. D misplaces the comma between the subject 'students' and its verb 'cheered', which illegally splits subject from predicate.

questions.stem: Which sentence does NOT contain a comma splice?

options.option_text: She loves cricket, she watches every match on television.
He studied all night, he passed the exam with great distinction.
Although it rained heavily, the match continued without any delay.
The sun set early, the temperature dropped significantly outside.

questions.explanation: C is correct: 'Although it rained heavily' is a dependent clause, so the comma separating it from the main clause is grammatically sound — not a splice. A, B, and D each join two independent clauses with only a comma, which defines a comma splice. They require a semicolon, a coordinating conjunction (FANBOYS), or a full stop to be grammatically complete.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses parentheses to enclose supplementary information?

options.option_text: The treaty (signed in 1648) ended the Thirty Years' War in Europe.
The treaty, (signed in 1648), ended the Thirty Years' War in Europe.
The treaty (signed in 1648,) ended the Thirty Years' War in Europe.
The treaty (signed in 1648.) ended the Thirty Years' War in Europe.

questions.explanation: A is correct: parentheses alone enclose the supplementary phrase with no flanking commas. B duplicates punctuation by adding commas both before and after the parenthetical. C places a comma inside the closing parenthesis, which is only permitted when the entire parenthetical is a standalone complete sentence. D inserts a full stop inside the parenthesis mid-sentence — that usage is reserved for a parenthetical that is itself a complete sentence and ends before the outer sentence closes.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly positions an exclamation mark in an exclamatory sentence?

options.option_text: What a remarkable! achievement the team has accomplished here.
What a remarkable achievement the team has accomplished here!
What a remarkable achievement! the team has accomplished here.
What! a remarkable achievement the team has accomplished here.

questions.explanation: B is correct because the entire exclamatory clause is one unit and the exclamation mark belongs at its close. A places it after 'remarkable', severing the adjective from its noun mid-phrase. C places it after 'achievement', leaving the remainder of the sentence without a terminal mark, and incorrectly lowercases the word that follows. D treats 'What' alone as a complete interjection, which changes both the grammar and the intended meaning of the sentence.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly punctuates 'however' functioning as a conjunctive adverb between two independent clauses?

options.option_text: The exam was difficult however, all the students passed with ease.
The exam was difficult; however, all the students passed with ease.
The exam was difficult, however all the students passed with ease.
The exam was difficult, however; all the students passed with ease.

questions.explanation: B is correct: a conjunctive adverb joining two independent clauses requires a semicolon before it and a comma after it. A omits the semicolon entirely, producing a run-on sentence. C uses only a comma before 'however', which is a classic comma splice — one of the most frequently tested errors in SSC CGL and IBPS English sections. D reverses the logic, placing the comma before 'however' and the semicolon after it, which is grammatically incoherent.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly punctuates a non-restrictive appositive phrase?

options.option_text: Dr. Kalam the former President of India was a renowned scientist.
Dr. Kalam, the former President of India, was a renowned scientist.
Dr. Kalam, the former President of India was a renowned scientist.
Dr. Kalam, the former President, of India was a renowned scientist.

questions.explanation: B is correct: a non-restrictive appositive must be enclosed by two commas — one opening and one closing — because it is removable supplementary information. A omits both commas, making the appositive appear restrictive and blurring meaning. C opens with a comma but never closes it, leaving an asymmetric and broken structure that misleads the reader about where the appositive ends. D splits 'President of India' at 'President', creating a false appositive and stranding 'of India' as an orphaned prepositional phrase.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly places a question mark when a direct question is embedded within a larger statement?

options.option_text: She asked, 'Are the results out,' and left the room in a hurry.
She asked, 'Are the results out?' and left the room in a hurry.
She asked, 'Are the results out'? and left the room in a hurry.
She asked, 'Are the results out?' And left the room in a hurry.

questions.explanation: B is correct: for a quoted direct question, the question mark belongs inside the closing quotation mark and no additional period follows, because the question mark already serves as terminal punctuation for the quoted clause. A substitutes a comma for the question mark, stripping the embedded clause of its interrogative character entirely. C places the question mark outside the closing quote, violating standard British and Indian exam punctuation conventions for embedded questions. D capitalises 'And' as though it begins a new sentence, incorrectly treating the continuation 'and left the room in a hurry' as syntactically independent.
